**Slides.** [Open the deck at this part](../../slides/housing-one-day-open-science.html#/part-1-credibility-and-open-research){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).

Part 1 asks what a claim in social science is for, why people describe the field as being in crisis, how three very large studies measured the problem, and what open research proposes as a remedy, down to the software, the archives and the registries that hold its materials. The part takes ninety minutes. The hands-on work comes at the end and runs into the first break, so that if your machine gives trouble you miss none of the talk.

## 1. The plan of the day

**On the slides.** The facilitator sets out the plan of the day and its two kinds of aim, what you will understand and what you will be able to do. The slides also say what you do not need: no installation, no git, and no GitHub or OSF account. Open the browser lab in a tab while the facilitator talks.

[Open the browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 2. The credibility of social science

**On the slides.** Follow the talk on what social science is for, on false positives and forking paths, and on the evidence from replications and many-analysts studies. It goes on to incentives and questionable research practices, which matter far more than fraud, and to the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset, with the estimates that they returned. It ends on why people speak of more than one 'replication' crisis.

## 3. The three Rs and open research

**On the slides.** The word 'replication' names three different operations, which the slides set out as a matrix of data against analysis. They then turn to repeatability and credibility, with a quick check on the matrix, and to the practices of open research, from open data to registered reports.

## 4. SCORE and Multi100

**On the slides.** The SCORE programme ran three studies, of reproducibility, robustness and replicability, and the slides give the results of each and the finding that the three do not travel together. They then present Multi100 from the position of an analyst inside it: what an analyst received, the two tasks, and how the results were put on a common scale.

## 5. The infrastructure of open research

**On the slides.** The slides cover open-source software, the toolchain, plain-text file formats and what happens when you render, the archives in which data and code are kept, the browser lab and the workspace, and what the tools cannot do. An optional run of five slides covers programming languages, editors, packages, version control and licences.

## 6. Task 1 and the warm-up

[Open the browser lab at Task 1](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-1-setup){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

Task 1 is the setup check. Wait for the R engine, run the setup cell and check that `audit` has 1,014 rows. Then go on to the [warm-up](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#warm-up), which asks you to name the R that each of four scenarios of the case describes, and one of the scenarios describes none of the three. If you have installed the workspace, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` in your IDE instead. If you need more time, carry on into the break.

**By the end of the part** you can tell apart the three operations that go under the single word 'replication', you know where the materials of a published study are kept and under which licences, and you have R running in the browser lab with the 1,014 emails of the housing-audit data loaded.
